display_title: Realistic setting, questions on experimental validation

content.title: Realistic setting, questions on experimental validation
content.review:
### Summary:

This paper proposes a method for solving the holographic phase retrieval problem (similar to classical phase retrieval but with a known reference) under realistic conditions of high noise levels and unavailable low-frequency data. 

The method incorporates the physical forward model into a Poisson likelihood objective function that allows a deep neural network deep decoder prior. Through a variety of experiments the authors compare their method against baselines and investigate when the neural network prior is particularly helpful.


########################################

### Strong points:

The paper considers a ractical setting which entails a beamstop and Poisson model. Moreover when learning is used, no training data is required which is useful in scientific imaging scenarios where training data may not be available.

The method is able to incorporate the physical forward model even when learning is used.

The Poisson model is experimentally compared against the more widely used MSE to justify the development of this Poisson-based method for handling low photon count scenarios.

The authors point out where learning is helpful and where it is not helpful via a variety of experiments.


########################################

### Weak points:

As the Poisson model and deep decoder are not new on their own, a thorough experimental evaluation is important:

\- Most of the results are for the three sample images. As the method performance varies depending on the image (as acknowledged by the authors in the paper), the conclusions would be strengthened by evaluating average performance over a larger set of images / signals. While Figure 15 shows this for one set of experiments, this is not done for the beamstop and separation experiments.

\- Following on, looking at generalization to other signals / images is especially critical as a separate deep decoder architecture (Table 1) was tuned for each of these three images. No validation set was used. In a practical setting we will not be able to tune the architecture according to the image that we wish to recover.

\- The authors vary the ill-posedness of the problem by varying the number of photons which is helpful. Are there also results on the performance of the method for other variations in ill-posedness (such as varying the oversampling ratio)?

Is there an error in Figure 15? The errors get worse as the photon count on the horizontal axis increases.

In Figure 4 and the other Figures for this type of experiment, why do the Wiener and inverse filtering errors start to fall as the beamstop area is increasing and the problem gets harder? Furthermore, there are sharp jumps in the HolOpt methods after a certain beamstop size when the number of photons is higher. Is there some critical threshold?


########################################

### Recommendation:

Overall I lean towards rejection. I like the more realistic setting as well and the examination of where the deep decoder is particularly helpful. However, the experimental validation should be strengthened to better understand the proposed method.


########################################

### Additional questions and clarifications that will help assessment:

Please address and clarify my above questions and queries.

One of the listed contributions (number ii) in Section 1.3 is the efficient auto-differentiation implementation. Please can the authors expand on the specific contributions and challenges that were overcome to do this?

A single reference is provided in section 1.1 for the beamstop. Please can the authors discuss and motivate the scenarios where a beamstop is used in more detail?


########################################

### Additional feedback that does not necessarily impact recommendation:

What is C in equation 2 / how is it determined for the experiments?

How is the random initialization for the deep decoder input done?

[Minor] The font size on the graph axes and some figures is quite small.

[Minor] Some references contain URLs (PyTorch one even extends beyond the margins) and others do not.

[Minor] For completeness it would be nice to state the MSE loss used in the experiments.

[Typo] Euclidian on page 13 section A.2


######### After author response #########

I thank the authors for their responses and updates to the manuscript which clarified some of my queries. However, I still feel that there are gaps in the experimental evaluation which impacts the understanding of the method from a machine learning perspective (e.g.  architecture / iterations is varied across noise levels according to Table 1). I retain my original score for this reason.
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

content.title: Response to AnonReviewer3
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the thorough remarks.

Indeed, the main text of the paper discusses reconstruction on three example images, chosen to have very different properties. The camera man image represents the class of photographic images, the virus image is an example of microscopic image, and the example taken from the COIL data set was selected for its tightly cropped non-cartesian image support and zeroed out background to make the phase retrieval problem harder to solve. It should be noted here that many contributions concerning machine learning in phase retrieval neglect the fact that the phase retrieval problem becomes much harder when the image support (its non-zero region) is not assumed known to pixel accuracy. In this sense, our three images cover a range of situations of interest, and their varying reconstruction accuracies and parameter settings are due to this fact. We chose the arguably hardest class of images to run a statistical analysis, which led to a section in the Appendix. With the page limit extension, we are able to bring these aggregate statistics (formerly Figure 15, now Figure 5) on the COIL data set to the main paper. Although other image datasets with non-trivial support, e.g. MNIST, are sometimes used in works on machine learning for phase retrieval, we eschewed such an “easy” (owing to its small image dimensions and simple structure) dataset in favor of larger and more realistic images.

Concerning the choice of deep decoder parameters, we note that related works report similar tuning (see e.g. Heckel, R., & Hand, P. (2019) tuning the number of channels to the level of noise in their experiment). We note further that the parameters selected for the single COIL1 image yielded good results on randomly selected COIL images from the rest of the dataset (see Figure 14 in the Appendix - please refer to the new numbering of Figures). 

The inclusion of a beamstop in our modeling is based on its practical necessity in Coherent Diffraction Imaging. Such a beamstop is required so as to allow the limited dynamic range inherent in CCD detectors to capture the broadest data spectrum possible. It is also often necessary to protect the detector array from being burned by extremely high-energy X-ray sources (He et al 2015, Marchesini et al 2008, Shechtman et al 2015). In reference to the reviewer’s question about apparent sharp increases in our methods’ errors at high noise levels and above certain beamstop area fractions, we are not aware at this time of any phenomenon that would cause a “critical threshold”. The log-scales may artificially make these jumps seem more or less salient at different noise levels.

The reviewer correctly identified an issue with Wiener filtering at small beamstop sizes: The reconstruction errors of Wiener- and inverse filtering are significantly degraded at small beamstop sizes. This is due to ringing of low frequencies and is inherent to the method used to fill the missing magnitudes before filtering. Although we tested a wide range of beamstop areas to understand the degradation of the reconstruction, it should be noted that the beamstop sizes at which this issue occurs are probably too small for any real-world setting.

Concerning varying the oversampling rate, this is a possible axis of parameter variation which we had not explored yet at the time of the submission. Please find an additional experiment in Section C of the Appendix where the oversampling rate is varied. Only the HIO baseline is applicable in this setting, as Wiener and inverse filtering each require at least 2x oversampling. We find that our methods produce superior reconstructions at the fixed noise level tested (1 photon/pixel), and thank the reviewer for calling attention to this setting.

We modified the wording in the text to avoid any misunderstanding about our usage of auto-differentiation. We are not claiming to have implemented a specific solution. On the contrary, we would like to point out that the existing efficient implementation makes our method immediately applicable to modifications in the forward model (such as the presence or absence of a beamstop or different assumptions of noise distribution). This is in contrast with many iterative algorithms (see for example Wang et al ICML 2020).

Many thanks to the reviewer for the suggested corrections and for catching errors in the manuscript. For the sake of time we have not proceeded yet, but we intend to update the text and graphs accordingly.

Lastly,  we hope to be able to provide additional experimental results within the next few days.

content.comment:
Answers to minor points:
- In our simulated data, the constant C in equation 2 is taken equal to the l1 norm of the observations Y. This normalization is necessary to interpret N_p as the number of incident photons. Note that neither C nor N_p ultimately appear in the objective function (3).
- The deep decoder latent representation is drawn from a standard normal distribution, and the layer parameters are initialized using the default Pytorch initialization. 

References:
- He, K., Sharma, M. K., & Cossairt, O. (2015). High dynamic range coherent imaging using compressed sensing. Optics Express, 23(24), 30904. 
- Heckel, R., & Hand, P. (2019). Deep Decoder: Concise Image Representations from Untrained Non-convolutional Networks. - International Conference on Learning Representations. 
- Marchesini et al, Massively parallel X-ray holography. Nature Photonics. 2008.
- Yoav Shechtman, Yonina C Eldar, Oren Cohen, Henry Nicholas Chapman, Jianwei Miao, andMordechai Segev. (2015) Phase retrieval with application to optical imaging: a contemporary overview. IEEE signal processing magazine, 32(3):87–109.
- Yaotian Wang, Xiaohang Sun, and Jason W. Fleischer. (2020) When deep denoising meets iterative phase retrieval. In International Conference on Machine Learning.

content.title: Response to author response
content.comment:
Thanks for addressing my queries.

The new and corrected Figure 5 (brought into the main paper) is useful in demonstrating the regime where learning helps (Figure is very pixelated especially when zoomed---please correct in next revision). As the other sample images have different characteristics to the COIL images, it could be useful to similarly study the regime where learning works for those image types.

Heckel, R., & Hand, P. (2019) introduced the deep decoder. The aim of this work is different---solve a practical scientific imaging problem where we do not know the image type or the noise level a priori. Furthermore we have no ground truth. Here however the architecture is tuned for each noise level and image. A practitioner would like to know how sensitive performance is to architecture mismatch. The architectures for COIL 100 experiments are still varied depending on the noise level. For example, what If you only had one (or very few) architecture(s) option(s)? And what can be done to make the solution less sensitive if it turns out to be sensitive?

Thank you for the experiments varying the oversampling ratio. Visually (Figure 34) the proposed method looks better and I believe this is a good addition to the paper. However, from the graphs (Figure 33) it might not be straightforward to say that the method is ‘superior’. Having some of these figures in the main paper may be worthwhile as they provide a different axis of ill-posedness.

I raise all these comments on the experiments because as reviewer 2 and I mention, the Poisson model and deep decoder are not new. Therefore in my opinion the experimental section should be strong and as practically relevant as possible (which was in fact the purpose of using the Poisson model, beamstop etc in the first place) to strengthen the contribution. Along these lines other takeaways or explanations for the performance of the learning method that are useful for the community are also helpful.

Thank you for the clarifications on the other queries about the beamstop, latent code etc---I think some of these should be added to the main manuscript. I see that you are trying to provide further experimental results and I will look at them if they are added.

content.title: Second round response
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their response. 

As listed in the global summary, we were able to add further experiments: namely the replication of the beamstop and reference separation experiments on the entire COIL100 dataset. 

Concerning the architecture of the deep decoder, we agree with the reviewer that it is important for a practitioner to understand its influence. The Appendix of the original submission contains an experiment (see Figure 10) showing the influence of depth (we found the number of channels to only marginally influence the reconstruction). In short, this experiment shows that the deeper the Deep Decoder the stronger the regularization towards smooth images. Thus choosing the depth of the network is akin to choosing a level of regularization. Regularization always incurs trade-off in regimes with imperfect information as the low-photon regime we propose to study here. In a setting where it would be impossible to tune the level of regularization (i.e. to test different architectures), a reasonable strategy would be to regularize little (i.e. to choose a shallow architecture with 1-2 layers or even reconstruct without any neural network prior, optimising directly on the pixels which is also one of the method we propose). Finally, we note that for the COIL100 experiments, we used the same architecture for the entire dataset for each noise level, despite only tuning the architecture based on the first image in the dataset, and still obtained good reconstruction results across images (see Figure 14). This validates that an architecture selected for one image generalizes well to a similar class of images. Thus, for a sequence of comparable imaging tasks, a practitioner only need select an architecture once (based on say the first image) before reconstructing the remaining samples without introducing any further bias. 

To resolve the discrepancy between the visual quality of samples and the metrics reported on graphs, as noted for instance by the reviewer for the oversampling experiment, we are interested in designing a perceptual metric in future work. As we noted in our response to AnonReviewer 4, this is a current area of research (see e.g. Zhang et al 2018). Nonetheless, for the oversampling experiment in particular, we emphasize that Figure 37 includes the full set of reconstructions pertaining to Figure 36. Thus, we are confident that our methods actually are fully superior in this setting, despite the suboptimality of MSE and SSIM as proxies for the “perceptual loss” . We have updated the text of Section C of the Appendix to make this more clear. 

- Zhang, R., Efros, A. A., Shechtman, E., & Wang, O. (2018). The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Deep Features as a Perceptual Metric. CVPR, 1, 13. 

Please let us know if we have adequately addressed your comments, and if you have any further questions.

display_title: Paper about more realistic phase retrieval

content.title: Paper about more realistic phase retrieval
content.review:
Summary: 
This paper studies the problem of phase retrieval. In contrast to previous work, this paper proposes to model the observations via a Poisson process, incorporates a beamstop, and also considers a variant with a known reference (holography). The resulting log-likelihood is tractable and optimized via gradient descent either in pixel space or in the parameter space of a deep image prior.

Strengths:
+ The addition of Poisson process and beamstop make the setting more realistic
+ The two algorithms (pixels, deep-decoder) show qualitatively different behavior. Deep-decoder can work with less data, but saturates, while the pixel space optimization requires more data but does not saturate.
+ Holography is a neat idea for improving performance of inverse problems. Although mature in the phase retrieval literature, this idea seems relatively under-explored in the recent neural-network-based approaches for inverse problems.

Concerns / weaknesses:
- Most plots in the main paper are created for single images making them and any interpretations only applicable to that image. It would be more useful to show plots averaged over a many images so that more robust comparisons between different approaches can be made.
- All results presented in the paper use simulated measurements. Given that the goal of this paper is to make phase retrieval practically applicable, the paper would be significantly stronger if the benefits of the proposed approach were to be demonstrated on a dataset with real measurements.
- At high noise levels, the qualitative and quantitative results seem to disagree. Why is this the case? Perhaps it would be useful to look at a perceptual similarity metric in addition to the L2 reconstruction error?
- In the text, it is discussed why baselines are sensitive to the separation parameter and why the proposed methods should not be . However, the empirical results show the opposite (Fig 6). Why is this the case?
- It would be nice to compare the results under a realistic (Poisson) measurement model with or without holography to quantify the benefits of holography for phase retrieval under the various approaches.
content.confidence: 3: The reviewer is fairly confident that the evaluation is correct

content.title: Response to AnonReviewer4
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their accurate summary of our contributions as well as the detailed remarks and suggestions.

It is correct that the main paper did not contain any aggregate statistics of performance of our method over a whole data set. This type of analysis was available in the appendix (formerly Figures 15 and 14; now Figures 5 (main) and 14). However, we would like to point out that our method can be applied to single images, which is one of its strengths in terms of applicability to a real-life experimental setting. To highlight this, we focused on showcasing results on three very different single images. (Please see answer to AnonReviewer3 for details on this selection.) With the page limit extension, we are able to bring the aggregate statistics on the COIL data set to the main paper. 

At the time of development of our method, we did not have suitable experimental data available to conduct an analysis in the real-world setting. However, we do plan such an analysis as future work. 

The reviewer aptly points out that there is a discrepancy between perceptual quality of the results and L2 error, the latter sometimes being higher for perceptually better reconstructions in the high-noise regime. This behavior also troubled us in the interim and we have evaluated performance of our reconstruction methods under SSIM (structural similarity metric) and have updated the paper with results (Figures 15, 18, and 21 in the Appendix). Although it constitutes an improvement, this measure still does not correlate perfectly with the perceptual quality of the reconstructed images. We note that designing perceptual metrics is an ongoing topic of research (Zhang et al 2018). As it appears, our brains are excellent at eliminating seemingly uniform noise over an image, while this is harder to implement systematically. The sum of these small errors over the entire image is arguably explaining the over-pessimistic evaluation of the MSE and to an extent SSIM.  
 
The reviewer also points out that in former Figure 6 (now Figure 8) our reconstruction method does not always beat the baseline at shorter holographic separation distances. We would like to point out firstly that the main baseline methods, inverse and Wiener filtering, we use for comparison cannot handle a reference separation lower than image support width. We therefore had to adapt a different baseline method, HIO, to the holographic case to have any point of comparison. In the text we make the point that reconstruction with the deep decoder is less sensitive than other methods to the separation  for VIRUS and CAMERA (Figure 8 top row and Figure 16 in the Appendix). We encountered a particularity with COIL1 where the deep decoder fails at very small separations, but beats the baseline after a given threshold separation smaller than the holographic-separation, for which we offer an interpretation in the text.

Finally, the reviewer suggests that we compare with non-holographic phase retrieval to quantify the benefits of holography in our various settings. We first emphasize that holographic phase retrieval and classical Fourier phase retrieval are mathematically very different problems (see response to AnonReviewer2 for more details), and in this work we chose to focus on the former. In the setting of imaging nanoscale objects such as viruses, the low-photon regime is greatly improved by the use of a holographic reference for reconstruction. We added an expository figure (Figure 1) showing the improvements due to use of holography and the Poisson likelihood for the low-photon regime.

- Zhang, R., Efros, A. A., Shechtman, E., & Wang, O. (2018). The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Deep Features as a Perceptual Metric. CVPR, 1, 13.

The paper proposes a Poisson maximum likelihood framework to  the holographic phase retrieval problem in the low-photon regime using untrained deep image prior.


1) The holographic phase retrieval problem studied in the paper might not be of great interest to the community of ICLR, so it is probably better to submit the paper to other venues.
2) In section 4, it would make the paper more self-contained if the author could list the size/statistics of the datasets used in the paper

replying_to: Replying to Seems that ICLR is not the most appropriate venue for this topic

content.title: Response to AnonReviewer1
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their comments. In reference to our works’ suitability for ICLR, we believe it is of interest to the ICLR community for several reasons. Broadly speaking, learning and representations are increasingly being applied to science, especially physical inverse problems (see for example Darestani, M. Z., & Heckel, R. 2020 and references therein for MRI applications). This contribution is a step in that direction, and falls firmly within the “applications” category of the conference topics. For phase retrieval in particular, there is significant overlap with the machine learning community, such as (Hand, P. et al NeurIPS 2018, Wang et al ICML 2020). Yet as noted by AnonReviewer4, holographic phase retrieval has remained relatively unexplored in the recent thrust towards deep learning for inverse problems, so we believe it is especially valuable to highlight our work in a machine learning venue.

More specifically, in presenting this work to the ICLR community our motives are multifold. We aim to narrow the gap between the type of questions in phase retrieval pursued by those from the machine learning community, and practical considerations faced by practitioners. For example, phase retrieval as it arises in practice involves strictly Fourier measurements with a fixed oversampling rate, Poisson noise with low photon counts, and a beamstop obscuring low frequencies. Moreover, classical phase retrieval is hopelessly ill-posed, whereas holography offers a more robust framework for imaging in practical high-noise settings (A. Barnett,  et al 2020); even within holography, the reference placement is an important experimental consideration (D. A. Barmherzig et al 2019). In contrast, highly cited works on phase retrieval better known to the machine learning community make no reference to holography or to a beamstop, and often assume Gaussian (instead of Fourier) measurement vectors or Gaussian (instead of Poisson) noise (C. Metzler et al 2018). The availability of a training set, whether labeled with correct phases or not, is also not common in practice. We are hopeful that our work will better illuminate a more practical model for phase retrieval, such that future works applying machine learning to phase retrieval can have the greatest potential impact on practice.

Indeed, we show that such practical considerations are not just a nuisance, but in fact overlooked facets of phase retrieval where machine learning may offer significant, previously unexplored advantages, such as a higher tolerance to challengingly close reference placement and to large beamstops. Moreover, the beamstop facet of phase retrieval may be of particular interest to the computer vision community because of its similarities to image inpainting, and machine learning approaches to fill or otherwise treat the missing low magnitudes are currently lacking from the literature.

Regarding the reviewer’s second comment, we note that the first paragraph of Section 4 is a “Data” paragraph describing the test images we use. A key advantage of our methods is that they are dataset-free, so figures in the main body of the paper correspond to precisely those three single images that are described in Section 4. With the page limit extension, we are able to bring the aggregate statistics on the full COIL data set from the Appendix to the main paper (see Figure 5).  We also fully describe this data set in the "Data" paragraph . If there are other relevant details or statistics that should be added to Section 4, we would be happy to add them.

- D. A. Barmherzig, J. Sun, P. N. Li, T. J. Lane and E. J. Candes, "Holographic phase retrieval and reference design," in Inverse Problems, vol. 35, no. 5. 2019.
- A. Barnett, C. Epstein, L. Greengard, J. Magland, Geometry of the phase retrieval problem. Inverse Problems, 2020, vol 36 no 9
- Darestani, M. Z., & Heckel, R. (2020). Can Un-trained Neural Networks Compete with Trained Neural Networks at Image Reconstruction? ArXiv Preprint, 2007.02471. 
- Paul Hand, Oscar Leong, and Vladislav Voroninski. Phase Retrieval Under a Generative Prior. In Neural Information Processing Systems 2018.
- C. Metzler, P. Schniter, A. Veeraraghavan, R. Baraniuk, prDeep: Robust Phase Retrieval with a Flexible Deep Network. Proceedings of the 35th Annual Conference on Machine Learning (2018)
- Yaotian Wang, Xiaohang Sun, and Jason W. Fleischer. When deep denoising meets iterative phase retrieval. In International Conference on Machine Learning, 2020.

display_title: The Poisson likelihood estimator is classical method for image recovery (contribution is not very significant)

content.title: The Poisson likelihood estimator is classical method for image recovery (contribution is not very significant)
content.review:
Summary: The paper presents a method to recover signal in a coherent diffraction imaging setup, where Fourier intensity of an unknown object and additive known reference is observed at the detector. In the low-light situation, measurement noise follows Poisson statistics. To recover signal from the measurements, the authors propose to use a Poisson maximum likelihood estimator. To further regularize the problem, the authors propose to use a deep decoder as an image prior. The paper presents simulation results on some sample images. 

Novelty and significance: It is a well-known fact in optics and signal processing that noise statistics in low light follow poisson distribution. The log-likelihood estimator for Poisson measurements is a standard optimization problem that is solved in such settings. In that respect I do not find the contributions of this paper novel or significant for publication. The paper uses a deep decoder as an image prior in the same Poisson estimator, which provides slight improvement in terms of reconstruction error. I do not consider that a significant or novel contribution of this paper, because similar ideas have been explored in other inverse problems. 

Correctness: The authors assume Poisson noise in the measurements, but then they compare their method with mean squared error-based optimization problems, which is not fair. Mean squared error-based optimization and weiner filter assume that noise is additive and Gaussian. I give that authors credit that they have discussed the relation between Poisson and Gaussian noise (i.e., in high photon count, the Poisson noise can be approximated with Gaussian), but including the comparisons and making claims that the proposed method performs better than classical methods is misleading. Poisson likelihood-based reconstruction is a classical method as well, and that is exactly what this paper is proposing. 

Quality: The paper is well written and I find it easy to read and understand. The experimental results are not impressive or surprising for the reasons I described above.
content.confidence: 5: The reviewer is absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct and very familiar with the relevant literature

replying_to: Replying to The Poisson likelihood estimator is classical method for image recovery (contribution is not very significant)

content.title: Response to AnonReviewer2
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their feedback. In reference to the novelty and significance, we agree that both the Poisson distribution of the measured magnitudes and maximum likelihood estimation are known as a general technique for image reconstruction. Indeed, existing works (such as Thibault, P., & Guizar-Sicairos, M. (2012)) have applied maximum likelihood estimation to classical phase retrieval. We thank the reviewer for hinting at such references, which we will add to our exposition to provide the reader a more complete picture of existing work. However, to the best of our knowledge, no work has previously considered maximum likelihood estimation for holographic phase retrieval under Poisson noise. (If this is not the case, we would be very grateful for a reference that already proposes and tests this technique for holographic phase retrieval.) Holographic phase retrieval is a fundamentally different image reconstruction setting from classical phase retrieval, despite their shared Poisson noise model: the holographic setting is generally well-conditioned (D. A. Barmherzig et al 2019), and indeed can be reduced to a linear inverse problem (in the noiseless or Gaussian noise cases), while ordinary phase retrieval is notoriously ill-conditioned and decisively non-linear. Accordingly, in the low-photon regime, the best reconstructions require a holographic reference and the corresponding maximum likelihood optimization for reconstruction (see newly added Figure 1). As such, the fact that maximum likelihood estimation has some precedent in ordinary phase retrieval does not discredit our work any more so than the existence of maximum likelihood estimation for other distinct imaging inverse problems.

With all of this considered, we believe our most fundamental contribution lies in applying Poisson maximum likelihood optimization to holographic phase retrieval, both with and without the deep decoder. Indeed, as was noted, the deep decoder sometimes provides a great advantage (when the photon count is very low, e.g. see two top rows of Figures 3, 11 and 12, and when the holographic separation is broken, e.g. see Figure 9 - please refer to the new numbering of Figures), while in other cases, optimizing the maximum likelihood objective alone achieves superior reconstruction. As highlighted as a strength by AnonReviewer3, investigating where learning is not helpful is also of scientific interest. 

The reviewer points out that we use a Poisson noise model in our method, yet compare with methods that use mean squared error-based optimization. We precisely compare to classical methods such as Inverse and Wiener filtering because they are often used under the wrong assumptions. We agree with the reviewer that it should be expected that these traditional methods are suboptimal in the studied regime. The point of our experiments is to provide experimental evidence to quantify the loss of performance due to the mismatch, over a wide range of noise levels.

In our work, we also emphasize two important practical aspects of the problem: missing low frequencies due to the beamstop, and reference-object distance breaking the holographic separation condition. In doing so, we highlight concrete and application-specific aspects of holography which are particularly well-suited to our Poisson-based maximum likelihood optimization frameworks and furthermore may be of interest to the broader machine learning community.

Broadly speaking, we believe it is important to adapt and test high-level concepts, which may have been introduced for other inverse problems, for practical and specific imaging modalities such as holographic phase retrieval: otherwise, such conceptual contributions are doomed to obscurity. The transition from proof of concept in a different inverse problem to actual application is not a triviality, as evidenced by e.g. the upcoming NeurIPS workshop on Deep Learning for Inverse Problems. 

- D. A. Barmherzig, J. Sun, P. N. Li, T. J. Lane and E. J. Candes, "Holographic phase retrieval and reference design," in Inverse Problems, vol. 35, no. 5. 2019. 
- Thibault, P., & Guizar-Sicairos, M. (2012). Maximum-likelihood refinement for coherent diffractive imaging. New Journal of Physics, 14.
- Y. Shechtman, Y. C. Eldar, O. Cohen, H. N. Chapman, J. Miao and M. Segev, "Phase Retrieval with Application to Optical Imaging: A contemporary overview," in IEEE Signal Processing Magazine, vol. 32, no. 3, pp. 87-109, May 2015, doi: 10.1109/MSP.2014.2352673.

content.title: Summary of changes made to the manuscript after feedback from reviewers
content.comment:
Following the point-by-point responses made individually to each reviewer, we summarize below the changes made to the submission based on their valuable feedback. 
- We added an introductory experiment to the paper (Figure 1) to succinctly demonstrate the power of holography combined with the proposed HolOpt strategy. The experiment compares the outcome of the reconstruction with or without a known reference, when performed either with the classical HIO algorithm or with the proposed HolOpt (four settings total). In short, the presence of a reference uniformly improves reconstruction for both algorithms, with the very best image quality requiring both a known reference and HolOpt. 
- We augment the evaluation of our experiments using the structural similarity index metric (SSIM) (Figures 15, 18, 19, 22, 24, 36 in the Appendix). Unfortunately, this metric was found not to be a significant improvement over the MSE for the prediction of the perceptual quality of the reconstruction.
- We provide more statistics on the full COIL dataset as requested. First, we moved Figure 5, originally in the Appendix, to the main body of the paper. Second, we replicated the experiments of Sections 4.2 (beamstop) and 4.3 (reference separation) on the entire COIL dataset (Figures 23 and 24 of the Appendix). These expanded experiments on the 100-image COIL dataset further validate our conclusions about the superiority of HolOpt to baseline methods in both traditional (noisy) and more challenging (missing low-frequency, close reference, and see below for reduced number of measurement) regimes. We note also that the deep decoder architecture was at no point modified for any of the other 99 images in the dataset, confirming that the same architecture works suitably well for similar images.
- Finally, we run an additional experiment, suggested by AnnonReviewer3, varying the oversampling ratio below and above the value of 2 (Section C of the Appendix, Figures 36 and 37).  (Note that we also ran this experiment on the full COIL dataset, such that all experiments in the paper have been validated on this larger set of images.) We find that our method outperforms significantly the HIO baseline -- which to our knowledge is the only baseline that applies in this setting -- in this challenging setting of small oversampling ratios. Little is known about uniqueness or recovery guarantees in this setting for the case of Fourier (rather than Gaussian) measurements, and the applicability and success of HolOpt here suggest a line of future work that may bridge the disparate lines of work on phase retrieval from the theory and imaging communities.
